extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic and philosophy
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook chapter analyzing the classification of 'namable things' and the nature/import of propositions: how propositions are formed, their types (affirmative/negative, simple/compound, categorical/hypothetical, universal/particular/indefinite/singular), the role of the copula, and competing accounts of propositional meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of Namable Things
rubrics_metrics.description: An enumeration and classification of all Namable Things: (1) Feelings or States of Consciousness; (2) The Minds which experience those feelings; (3) The Bodies, or external objects which excite certain of those feelings (together with powers/properties); (4) The Successions and Co-existences, the Likenesses and Unlikenesses between feelings or states of consciousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four classes are said to compose the signification of all names and whatever we call a fact. Distinguishes psychological/subjective facts (composed solely of states of consciousness) from objective facts (composed wholly or in part of substances and attributes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Feelings taxonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Feelings are of four sorts: Sensations, Thoughts, Emotions, and Volitions; Perceptions are a particular case of Belief; Actions are volitions followed by an effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text treats feelings as distinct from the objects which excite them and from the organs by which they are conveyed; this taxonomy underpins later predication and propositional analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substances: Bodies and Minds
rubrics_metrics.description: Substances are either Bodies or Minds. All we can know of Matter is the sensations it gives us and the order of their occurrence; Body is the unknown cause of our sensations, Mind the unknown recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The account acknowledges metaphysical doubts about Matter and Mind but adopts this epistemic stance as sufficient for logical purposes: substances figure in objective facts only insofar as they relate to sensations or states of consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attributes: Quality, Relation, Quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Attributes are of three kinds—Quality, Relation, and Quantity—and are grounded on sensations or other states of consciousness. Relations (except simple likeness/unlikeness, succession/simultaneity) are grounded on some fact or phenomenon (series of sensations). Quantity is grounded in differences in sensations produced by bulk or intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although attributes are in effect sensations or states of feeling (or inextricably involved with them), certain relations (likeness, succession, simultaneity) are so fundamentally distinct that they are classed apart for practical purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposition basics: subject, predicate, and the copula
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposition is a portion of discourse in which a predicate is affirmed or denied of a subject. The copula (commonly a form of 'to be' or an inflection) serves as the sign that distinguishes predication from mere juxtaposition of names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clear understanding of the copula's nature and office is important; confusion about the copula has historically led to mysticism and logomachy in logic. Inflection (e.g., 'burn' → 'burns') can serve the function but the copula is most common.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copula does not necessarily assert existence
rubrics_metrics.description: Using 'is' as a copula does not imply affirmation of existence: e.g., 'A centaur is a fiction of the poets' does not assert that a centaur exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The word 'to be' has a double meaning (copula vs existence), and failing to distinguish these meanings has caused much futile metaphysical speculation. The copula's grammatical role should not be conflated with existential claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affirmative vs Negative propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions divide into affirmative (predicate affirmed of subject, e.g., 'Cæsar is dead') and negative (predicate denied of subject, e.g., 'Cæsar is not dead'); the copula in negatives consists of words 'is not'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some logicians (e.g., Hobbes) treat negation as part of the predicate (so 'not dead' is the predicate). The author argues this confounds a real factual distinction (presence vs absence) with a merely verbal one and tends to obscure the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tense and modality attach to the copula
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences of tense (past, present, future) properly attach to the copula (the sign of predication) rather than to the predicate; modal expressions ('may', 'perhaps', 'possible') often express the state of our mind (absence of disbelief) rather than a property of the fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., 'The sun did rise', 'is rising', 'will rise'—these designate differences belonging to the event asserted and are properly considered as attaching to the copula. Modal phrases are assertions about our degree of certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple vs Compound (Complex) propositions and categorical/hypothetical/disjunctive forms
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple proposition affirms/denies one predicate of one subject. A compound/complex proposition contains more than one subject or predicate, but often is merely an aggregation of multiple propositions joined by conjunctions. Hypothetical (conditional) and disjunctive forms are special: conditional asserts an inferability relation, disjunctive is reducible to conditionals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many so-called complex propositions are really multiple propositions (e.g., 'Cæsar is dead, and Brutus is alive'). Hypothetical propositions are not mere aggregations; they concern propositions as subjects and predicates (see separate entry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothetical (conditional) propositions predicate of propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: In a hypothetical proposition the subject and predicate are names of propositions; the predicate is a general relative name applicable to propositions (e.g., 'an inference from so and so'). The assertion is that one proposition is a legitimate inference from another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: E.g., 'If A is B, C is D' abbreviates 'The proposition C is D is a legitimate inference from the proposition A is B.' This shows particles (if, and, but, or) act as abbreviations of propositional relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disjunction is resolvable into conditionals
rubrics_metrics.description: A disjunctive proposition ('Either A is B or C is D') is equivalent to conditional propositions: 'if A is not B, C is D' and 'if C is not D, A is B'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supports the view that hypothetical/conditional and disjunctive forms are closely related (often used synonymously with 'hypothetical').

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal / Particular / Indefinite / Singular classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Propositions are classified by the generality of the subject: Universal (predicate of all members, e.g., 'All men are mortal'), Particular (predicate of some portion, e.g., 'Some men are wise'), Indefinite (where expression doesn't clearly show universal vs particular — often a solecism), and Singular (subject is an individual name, e.g., 'Julius Cæsar is mortal').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context or custom often supplies universality when words omit explicit quantifiers. Examples illustrate 'indefinite' mainly arises with material names where subject can be universal or particular in different contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution as definition of universality/particularity
rubrics_metrics.description: A general name is 'distributed' when it stands for each and every individual it denotes. A universal proposition is one in which the subject is distributed; a particular proposition has an undistributed subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'All men are mortal' — subject 'man' is distributed. 'Some men are mortal' — both subject and predicate are undistributed. The notion of distribution is useful in stating syllogistic rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Import of propositions: about things, not mere ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The import (meaning) of propositions concerns the things themselves (facts in external nature), not merely the ideas or mental acts of judging. When one believes 'gold is yellow' the proposition refers to external phenomena, not solely to the ideas of gold and yellow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes doctrines that reduce propositions to relations between ideas or conceptions, arguing such views have impeded progress in logic by focusing on ideas rather than the objects/events propositions are about.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hobbes' account of propositional meaning (predicate as name of same thing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hobbes: in every proposition what is signified is the speaker's belief that the predicate is a name of the same thing of which the subject is a name (e.g., 'All men are living beings' true because 'living being' is a name of every thing 'man' is a name of).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text concedes this property is necessary for truth and is rigorously true in some cases (notably when both terms are proper names) but argues it is only a minute fragment of meaning; many propositions assert more than this collocational relation between names.
